declarations.name: EL_CORE_PRACTICES
declarations.source:
var EL_CORE_PRACTICES = [
    {
      id: 'crew_as_heart',
      practice: 'Crew as the heart of school',
      domain: 'culture',
      description: 'Crew is a small, multi-year advisory group of 10-15 students that meets daily or several times per week. The crew leader (a teacher) stays with the same students for multiple years, creating sustained relationships. Crew is where students set goals, track HOWLs, celebrate growth, and process challenges. The phrase "We are crew, not passengers" comes from Outward Bound co-founder Kurt Hahn.',
      whyItMatters: 'Belonging is the precondition for learning. When every student is known well by at least one adult, attendance rises, behavior referrals fall, and academic risk-taking increases. Crew is the structural answer to anonymity in middle and high school.',
      howlAlignment: ['responsibility', 'compassion', 'integrity', 'perseverance'],
      classroomLook: 'Circle of chairs. A check-in question (one word, fist-to-five, weather report). A HOWL focus for the week. Time for a goal review, a problem-solve, or a celebration. Closing ritual.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Treating crew as study hall or homeroom (kills the relational core)',
        'Rotating crew leaders annually (severs continuity)',
        'Skipping crew when academics feel pressed (signals it does not matter)',
        'Adult-led monologue instead of student voice'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, The Power of Crew (2021); Hahn, K., Outward Bound origins.'
    },
    {
      id: 'character_infused_curriculum',
      practice: 'Character infused throughout curriculum',
      domain: 'character',
      description: 'Character is not a separate class or assembly. It is taught and assessed inside academic work. A literature unit asks students to practice empathy as a reading skill. A science expedition asks students to practice integrity in data collection. HOWLs appear on rubrics next to academic standards.',
      whyItMatters: 'Character taught in isolation rarely transfers. Character practiced inside the work students already do becomes the work. This is the EL move that distinguishes it from add-on SEL programs.',
      howlAlignment: ['responsibility', 'compassion', 'integrity', 'perseverance'],
      classroomLook: 'A rubric with three columns: content knowledge, skills, and HOWLs. Students self-assess on all three. Teachers give feedback on all three. Report cards reflect all three.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Making HOWLs a behavior score (compliance, not character)',
        'Reducing HOWLs to participation points',
        'Inflating HOWL scores to avoid hard conversations',
        'Treating character as a separate weekly lesson'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Leaders of Their Own Learning (2014); Berger, R., An Ethic of Excellence (2003).'
    },
    {
      id: 'learning_expeditions',
      practice: 'Learning expeditions',
      domain: 'curriculum',
      description: 'An expedition is a long-term (6-12 week), in-depth study of a single compelling topic. Expeditions integrate multiple disciplines, include fieldwork and experts, and culminate in a product or performance for an audience beyond the teacher. They are the structural unit of EL curriculum.',
      whyItMatters: 'Expeditions answer the student question "Why are we learning this?" by making the answer visible. Real audience, real product, real consequence. Engagement and retention both rise.',
      howlAlignment: ['perseverance', 'responsibility', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'A guiding question on the wall ("How does water shape our town?"). A timeline of fieldwork dates, expert visits, and product deadlines. Drafts in progress. A countdown to the final presentation.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Calling a 2-week project an expedition (depth requires time)',
        'No real audience (a parent night does not always count)',
        'Skipping fieldwork or experts (the practice loses its anchor)',
        'Teacher-chosen topic with no student inquiry'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Transformational Literacy (2014); Mitchell, S., Expeditionary Learning case studies.'
    },
    {
      id: 'fieldwork',
      practice: 'Fieldwork',
      domain: 'curriculum',
      description: 'Fieldwork is purposeful, repeated learning outside the classroom. Students visit a salt marsh weekly to measure tide and species. They interview elders at a senior center. They map their neighborhood. Fieldwork is not a field trip; it is data collection, observation, and relationship-building tied to a guiding question.',
      whyItMatters: 'The classroom is a limited environment for learning about a non-classroom world. Fieldwork builds observation skills, sense of place, and the kind of evidence students cannot get from a textbook.',
      howlAlignment: ['responsibility', 'perseverance'],
      classroomLook: 'Clipboards, field guides, data sheets. A pre-fieldwork mini-lesson on what to look for. A post-fieldwork debrief and data entry. Photos and sketches in a field journal.',
      pitfalls: [
        'One-off trips with no return visit (loses the longitudinal data)',
        'No purpose beyond "fun" (students cannot connect it to the expedition)',
        'Unsafe or inaccessible sites (excludes students)',
        'Skipping the debrief (data sits in notebooks unused)'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Field Guide to Crew (2020); Sobel, D., Place-Based Education (2004).'
    },
    {
      id: 'experts',
      practice: 'Community experts as co-teachers',
      domain: 'curriculum',
      description: 'Experts are community members with real knowledge of the expedition topic who teach alongside the teacher. A welder visits the materials science unit. A nurse visits the health expedition. A poet workshops drafts. Experts make learning real and connect students to careers and community.',
      whyItMatters: 'Teachers cannot be experts in everything. Bringing in real practitioners signals to students that their work matters to the world, not just to school. It also widens the adult network around each student.',
      howlAlignment: ['responsibility', 'compassion'],
      classroomLook: 'A guest in the room demonstrating, answering student-prepared questions, critiquing student work, or guiding a small group. Thank-you notes that name specific things learned.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Treating experts as entertainers (one-shot talk, no integration)',
        'Not preparing students with questions (wastes expert time)',
        'Always the same demographic of experts (signals who counts)',
        'No follow-up communication (experts feel used)'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Core Practices (2018); Wiggins, G., Authentic Education (1989).'
    },
    {
      id: 'service_learning',
      practice: 'Service learning',
      domain: 'character',
      description: 'Service learning is academic work that meets a real community need. Students do not volunteer for community service hours; they apply what they are learning to solve a problem. A statistics class analyzes data for a local nonprofit. A history class restores a forgotten cemetery. Reflection is built in.',
      whyItMatters: 'Service without learning is volunteerism. Learning without service can feel pointless. Together they teach students that knowledge has consequences and that they are agents in their community now, not later.',
      howlAlignment: ['compassion', 'responsibility', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'A partnership agreement with a community organization. A project plan with deliverables. Reflection prompts after each service session. A final product the community can use.',
      pitfalls: [
        'One-off service days (no learning, no relationship)',
        'Saviorism framing (we are helping "those" people)',
        'No reflection (service becomes a chore)',
        'No partnership voice in project design'
      ],
      research: 'Eyler, J. & Giles, D., Wheres the Learning in Service-Learning? (1999); EL Education, Service Learning Guide (2019).'
    },
    {
      id: 'student_led_conferences',
      practice: 'Student-led conferences',
      domain: 'culture',
      description: 'At the end of each trimester, students lead a conference with their family and crew leader. They present a portfolio of work, narrate their growth on HOWLs and academics, share evidence, and set next-quarter goals. The student talks. The adults listen and ask questions.',
      whyItMatters: 'Traditional parent-teacher conferences leave the student out of the conversation about their own learning. Student-led conferences put the student in the driver seat and require them to own their growth.',
      howlAlignment: ['responsibility', 'integrity', 'perseverance'],
      classroomLook: 'Student-prepared portfolio (paper or digital). Student opens with a goal review, walks through work samples, names struggles and successes, sets new goals. Adults reflect back.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Reading from a script (no authentic reflection)',
        'No preparation time (students freeze)',
        'Teachers taking over (defeats the purpose)',
        'Skipping for students with low attendance (worst-served, most need it)'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Leaders of Their Own Learning (2014); Berger, R., et al., student-led conference protocols.'
    },
    {
      id: 'public_presentations',
      practice: 'Public presentations of learning',
      domain: 'culture',
      description: 'Every expedition ends with students presenting their work to a real audience beyond the teacher: a community panel, a published book, a museum exhibit, a city council briefing. The audience is not the parents in folding chairs; it is people who will use or be affected by the work.',
      whyItMatters: 'When work matters to a real audience, quality goes up. Students draft and revise without prodding. They care about precision because someone outside school will see it.',
      howlAlignment: ['perseverance', 'integrity', 'responsibility'],
      classroomLook: 'A presentation rubric co-created with students. Practice runs with peer feedback. A formal audience event with Q&A. Audience artifacts (programs, displays, published work) that signal real stakes.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Captive audience (other students forced to watch)',
        'No Q&A (kills the real-audience pressure)',
        'Only top students present (signals quality is for some)',
        'No revision time after practice runs'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Models of Excellence (2017); Berger, R., An Ethic of Excellence (2003).'
    },
    {
      id: 'models_of_excellence',
      practice: 'Models of excellence',
      domain: 'instruction',
      description: 'Before students attempt a piece of work, teachers show them models of excellent work, often by other students, sometimes professional. The class analyzes what makes the model excellent and co-creates the rubric from that analysis. Models make quality visible.',
      whyItMatters: 'Students cannot reach a standard they cannot see. "Be more descriptive" means nothing. A model of descriptive writing, dissected, gives students a target they can aim at.',
      howlAlignment: ['perseverance', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'A model under a document camera. Students annotate it. The class names the qualities of excellence. A rubric emerges from student observation, not from the teacher.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Only one model (looks like the right answer)',
        'Models too perfect (intimidate rather than inspire)',
        'No analysis (students copy surface features)',
        'No critique culture (models feel like judgment)'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Models of Excellence website; Wiggins, G., Educative Assessment (1998).'
    },
    {
      id: 'critique_and_revision',
      practice: 'Critique and revision',
      domain: 'instruction',
      description: 'Drafts are not the end of learning; they are the start. EL classrooms run regular critique sessions where students give and receive specific, kind, and helpful feedback. Students revise multiple times. Final work is the product of many drafts, not a first attempt.',
      whyItMatters: 'First drafts are first drafts. Quality lives in revision. Teaching the critique-revise cycle teaches students that their first attempt is not their best.',
      howlAlignment: ['perseverance', 'integrity', 'compassion'],
      classroomLook: 'A critique protocol on the wall (kind, specific, helpful). Drafts numbered (Draft 1, Draft 2, Draft 3). Visible revision marks. A final piece next to early drafts to show growth.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Vague feedback ("good job")',
        'Harsh feedback (kills risk-taking)',
        'Single revision (does not build the habit)',
        'No protected revision time (revision becomes homework)'
      ],
      research: 'Berger, R., An Ethic of Excellence (2003); EL Education, Austins Butterfly video.'
    },
    {
      id: 'reading_is_thinking',
      practice: 'Reading is thinking',
      domain: 'instruction',
      description: 'EL Education treats reading as an active, visible thinking process. Students annotate, question, summarize, and discuss texts using protocols like Text-Based Discussion, Marking the Text, or Save the Last Word. Reading is not silent and solitary; it is the engine of inquiry.',
      whyItMatters: 'Many students decode without comprehending. Making thinking visible during reading builds comprehension, vocabulary, and engagement with ideas.',
      howlAlignment: ['perseverance', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'Texts with student annotations. Sticky notes in margins. A discussion circle where students cite text. A reading log that tracks not just pages but thinking.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Round-robin reading (kills comprehension)',
        'No discussion (reading stays private)',
        'Only fiction (nonfiction is half of literacy)',
        'Texts too easy or too hard (no productive struggle)'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Reading Foundations (2017); Tovani, C., I Read It But I Dont Get It (2000).'
    },
    {
      id: 'productive_struggle',
      practice: 'Productive struggle',
      domain: 'instruction',
      description: 'Productive struggle is the experience of working at the edge of ability, not knowing the answer, and persisting through confusion. EL classrooms deliberately design tasks that require productive struggle. Teachers resist rescuing students too soon.',
      whyItMatters: 'Struggle that resolves builds confidence and skill. Rescue prevents both. The brain grows at the edge of competence, not in comfortable territory.',
      howlAlignment: ['perseverance', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'Open-ended problems. Wait time of 10+ seconds. Teacher questions instead of answers. Students using each other before they use the teacher. Visible thinking, including mistakes.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Unproductive struggle (too hard, no entry point)',
        'Rescuing too soon (signals "I dont believe you can")',
        'No safety net (struggle becomes shame)',
        'No celebration of mistakes (closes the door on risk)'
      ],
      research: 'Hiebert, J. & Grouws, D., Effects of Classroom Mathematics Teaching (2007); EL Education, Math Foundations.'
    },
    {
      id: 'cooperative_learning',
      practice: 'Cooperative learning structures',
      domain: 'instruction',
      description: 'Group work is not just sitting near each other. EL classrooms use structured cooperative learning protocols (Jigsaw, Numbered Heads, Think-Pair-Share, Fishbowl) that ensure every student contributes and every student is accountable. Roles are clear and rotated.',
      whyItMatters: 'Unstructured group work lets some students do all the work and others coast. Structured protocols distribute thinking, voice, and accountability.',
      howlAlignment: ['responsibility', 'compassion'],
      classroomLook: 'Visible protocol cards. Defined roles (facilitator, recorder, timekeeper, reporter). Every student speaks. A debrief on both content and process.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Calling pair work "groupwork" (no real cooperation)',
        'Same roles every time (some students never lead)',
        'No accountability (free riders)',
        'No process debrief (collaboration skills do not improve)'
      ],
      research: 'Johnson, D. & Johnson, R., Learning Together and Alone (1999); EL Education, Collaborative Learning protocols.'
    },
    {
      id: 'peer_critique',
      practice: 'Peer critique',
      domain: 'instruction',
      description: 'Peer critique is structured feedback among students using the kind-specific-helpful framework. Students learn to give critique that is honest about quality without crushing the maker. They also learn to receive critique without defensiveness. This is a teachable skill, not a personality trait.',
      whyItMatters: 'Teacher feedback is one voice. Peer feedback gives students multiple perspectives and builds their evaluative judgment. It also relieves teacher feedback bottlenecks.',
      howlAlignment: ['compassion', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'A critique sentence stem chart on the wall. Pairs or trios with one persons work in the middle. Specific, evidence-based comments. The maker takes notes and decides what to revise.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Vague compliments (no growth signal)',
        'Personal attacks (kills culture)',
        'No follow-up revision (critique becomes a chore)',
        'Teacher absent (no scaffolding when it goes off the rails)'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Critique and Feedback (2018); Berger, R., An Ethic of Excellence (2003).'
    },
    {
      id: 'habits_of_discussion',
      practice: 'Habits-of-discussion routines',
      domain: 'instruction',
      description: 'Strong discussion is taught, not assumed. EL classrooms use sentence stems, hand signals, and accountability moves to teach students how to build on each others ideas, disagree respectfully, ask probing questions, and bring quiet voices in. Discussion is a skill.',
      whyItMatters: 'Without taught habits, discussion devolves into a few loud voices and many silent ones. Habits of discussion distribute talk and deepen thinking.',
      howlAlignment: ['compassion', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'Sentence stems on the wall ("I agree with X because...", "Im not sure I follow, can you say more?"). A talk-tally chart tracking who has spoken. Wait time. Cold-calling with care.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Same students dominating (no protocol enforcement)',
        'Stems used mechanically (no real meaning)',
        'No debrief on discussion quality (skill does not develop)',
        'Cold-calling that shames'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Habits of Discussion; Lemov, D., Teach Like a Champion (2010).'
    },
    {
      id: 'family_partnerships',
      practice: 'Family-school partnerships',
      domain: 'culture',
      description: 'Families are not just informed; they are partners. EL schools host family literacy nights, expedition kickoffs, student-led conferences, and home visits. Communication is two-way and frequent. Families help shape, not just witness, their childs education.',
      whyItMatters: 'Schools that partner with families show better attendance, behavior, and academic outcomes. Families are the longest relationship a student has; schools are temporary collaborators.',
      howlAlignment: ['responsibility', 'compassion'],
      classroomLook: 'Translated communications. Family input on expedition topics. Home visits in the first month. Expedition products families can use. Conferences scheduled when families can attend.',
      pitfalls: [
        'One-way communication (school talks, families listen)',
        'Only English (excludes multilingual families)',
        'Daytime-only events (excludes working families)',
        'Treating families as compliance enforcers, not partners'
      ],
      research: 'Henderson, A. & Mapp, K., A New Wave of Evidence (2002); EL Education, Family Partnerships.'
    },
    {
      id: 'restorative_practices',
      practice: 'Restorative practices',
      domain: 'culture',
      description: 'When harm happens, the response is to repair relationships, not just punish. Restorative circles, affective questions, and reentry conversations are routine. Suspension and exclusion are last resorts. The questions are "Who was harmed?" and "What needs to happen to repair?", not "What rule was broken?"',
      whyItMatters: 'Punitive discipline removes students from the community that could change them. It also disproportionately harms students of color and students with disabilities. Restorative practice keeps students in school and rebuilds trust.',
      howlAlignment: ['compassion', 'responsibility', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'Circle structure for harm conversations. Affective statements ("When you did X, I felt Y"). A reentry meeting after any removal. No public shaming. Clear repair plan.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Restorative theater without restorative substance',
        'No skill-building (students lack the language)',
        'Inconsistent application across student groups',
        'No staff training (circles done badly cause more harm)'
      ],
      research: 'Costello, B., Wachtel, J., Wachtel, T., The Restorative Practices Handbook (2009); Gregory, A., et al., RP outcome studies.'
    },
    {
      id: 'just_right_challenge',
      practice: 'Just-right challenge',
      domain: 'instruction',
      description: 'Tasks are deliberately set in the zone of proximal development: hard enough to require effort, accessible enough to be reachable with scaffolding. Teachers differentiate the entry point, not the destination. All students work toward the same high standard.',
      whyItMatters: 'Tasks too easy bore. Tasks too hard defeat. Just-right tasks build both skill and identity as a capable learner.',
      howlAlignment: ['perseverance', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'Tiered entry points to the same task. Scaffolds available, not assigned. Quick formative checks. Adjustments mid-lesson based on student response.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Tracking disguised as differentiation',
        'Lowering expectations for some students',
        'Scaffolds that become crutches (never removed)',
        'No formative checks (mismatch never caught)'
      ],
      research: 'Vygotsky, L., Mind in Society (1978); EL Education, Differentiation guidance.'
    },
    {
      id: 'engaging_texts',
      practice: 'Engaging, complex texts',
      domain: 'curriculum',
      description: 'EL curriculum centers complex, beautiful, relevant texts. Students wrestle with primary sources, real literature, and topical nonfiction. Texts are chosen for both rigor and engagement, not just one or the other. Texts about real people doing real things appear in every grade.',
      whyItMatters: 'Reading skill grows from reading hard things with support. Watered-down texts produce watered-down readers. Engaging topics produce readers who choose to keep reading.',
      howlAlignment: ['perseverance', 'compassion'],
      classroomLook: 'A diverse classroom library. Texts at and above grade level with scaffolding. Discussion of why a text matters. Student choice within a curated set.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Texts that do not reflect students lives',
        'Avoiding hard texts (lowers ceiling)',
        'Forcing every student through the same text without supports',
        'Cultural tokenism in text selection'
      ],
      research: 'Common Core text complexity research; EL Education, Reading Foundations (2017).'
    },
    {
      id: 'learning_targets',
      practice: 'Student-friendly learning targets',
      domain: 'instruction',
      description: 'Every lesson opens with a learning target in student-friendly language, typically "I can..." statements tied to a standard. Students reference the target throughout the lesson and self-assess against it at the end. Targets are short, specific, and visible.',
      whyItMatters: 'Students who know what they are learning learn more than students who do not. Clear targets give students agency in their own learning.',
      howlAlignment: ['responsibility', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'A visible "I can" statement on the board. A mid-lesson check-in. An end-of-lesson self-assessment (thumbs, exit ticket, traffic light).',
      pitfalls: [
        'Targets written but not used',
        'Targets too vague to assess',
        'Targets in teacher language ("SWBAT analyze...")',
        'No closing self-assessment'
      ],
      research: 'Hattie, J., Visible Learning (2009); EL Education, Leaders of Their Own Learning (2014).'
    },
    {
      id: 'tracking_progress',
      practice: 'Tracking progress',
      domain: 'instruction',
      description: 'Students keep visible track of their own progress on academic standards and HOWLs. Goal-setting and progress monitoring are routine, not exceptional. Students see growth over time, not just current grades.',
      whyItMatters: 'Tracking makes the invisible visible. Students who see their own growth develop self-efficacy and a growth mindset.',
      howlAlignment: ['responsibility', 'integrity', 'perseverance'],
      classroomLook: 'A goal-tracking sheet in each binder. A growth-over-time chart on the wall. A weekly goal-review crew meeting. Evidence of progress, not just numbers.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Tracking that becomes shaming (public rankings)',
        'Tracking only deficit (where students fall short)',
        'No reflection (numbers without meaning)',
        'No goal-setting (tracking without forward motion)'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Leaders of Their Own Learning (2014); Dweck, C., Mindset (2006).'
    },
    {
      id: 'celebrations_of_learning',
      practice: 'Celebrations of learning',
      domain: 'culture',
      description: 'EL schools regularly celebrate learning in public ways: portfolio nights, expedition exhibits, all-school assemblies. Celebrations are for growth and effort, not just achievement. The point is to make learning visible and valued.',
      whyItMatters: 'What schools celebrate signals what schools value. Celebrating learning, effort, and growth reshapes the culture.',
      howlAlignment: ['compassion', 'perseverance'],
      classroomLook: 'A schedule of celebration events. Family invitations. Student work on walls. Names called for specific growth, not just top scores. Snacks.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Only celebrating the top',
        'Generic celebration (no specific growth named)',
        'Celebration without rigor (everyone gets a trophy hollow)',
        'No family invitation'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Core Practices (2018).'
    },
    {
      id: 'structures_for_voice',
      practice: 'Structures for student voice',
      domain: 'leadership',
      description: 'EL schools build formal structures for student voice: student government, advisory councils, climate surveys, student-led professional development. Voice is structural, not just rhetorical. Students help govern the school.',
      whyItMatters: 'Students who help shape the school they attend are more invested in it. They also bring expertise adults lack about the student experience.',
      howlAlignment: ['responsibility', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'A student council that meets with leadership. Student-designed climate surveys. Students on hiring panels. Student-led PD sessions.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Tokenism (one student on a committee for show)',
        'Limited issues (students "voice" cafeteria menus only)',
        'No follow-through (voice gathered, never acted on)',
        'Only "easy" students invited (excludes critique)'
      ],
      research: 'Mitra, D., Student Voice and Student Engagement (2007); EL Education, Student Leadership.'
    },
    {
      id: 'two_teacher_planning',
      practice: 'Co-planning and shared accountability',
      domain: 'leadership',
      description: 'EL teachers plan in teams, not in isolation. Grade-level and content teams meet weekly to design expeditions, analyze student work, and adjust instruction. Teaching is treated as collective, not solo, practice.',
      whyItMatters: 'Solo teaching limits learning to a single adults perspective. Team planning multiplies expertise and creates shared accountability for every student.',
      howlAlignment: ['responsibility', 'compassion'],
      classroomLook: 'Protected team-planning time. Shared expedition documents. Student work walked through together. Norms for honest professional dialogue.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Planning time hijacked for logistics',
        'No norms (meetings become venting)',
        'No accountability (decisions not followed through)',
        'Hierarchical dynamics that silence newer teachers'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Teacher Leadership; Hargreaves, A. & Fullan, M., Professional Capital (2012).'
    },
    {
      id: 'protocols_for_looking_at_student_work',
      practice: 'Protocols for looking at student work',
      domain: 'leadership',
      description: 'EL teachers regularly examine student work together using structured protocols (Tuning Protocol, ATLAS, Consultancy). The goal is not to grade but to understand what students know, where they struggle, and how to adjust instruction.',
      whyItMatters: 'Student work is the truest data we have. Structured protocols keep the conversation focused on learning, not on personalities.',
      howlAlignment: ['integrity', 'responsibility'],
      classroomLook: 'A protocol agenda. A timekeeper. The teacher presenting work and a question. Colleagues offering warm and cool feedback. A debrief on next steps.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Skipping the protocol (conversation drifts)',
        'No question from the presenting teacher (no focus)',
        'Cool feedback as personal critique',
        'No follow-up (insights not acted on)'
      ],
      research: 'School Reform Initiative protocols; EL Education, Looking at Student Work.'
    },
    {
      id: 'instructional_leadership',
      practice: 'Instructional leadership rounds',
      domain: 'leadership',
      description: 'School leaders regularly visit classrooms not to evaluate but to learn. Rounds focus on a problem of practice, gather low-inference observations, and feed back to the whole staff. The goal is collective improvement, not individual judgment.',
      whyItMatters: 'Walkthroughs that evaluate make teachers defensive. Walkthroughs that learn build trust and improve instruction.',
      howlAlignment: ['integrity', 'responsibility'],
      classroomLook: 'A small team of leaders/teachers walking together. A focus question on a sticky note. Low-inference notes. A debrief that surfaces patterns, not individuals.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Confusing rounds with evaluation',
        'Naming individual teachers in debriefs',
        'No focus question (notes drift)',
        'No follow-up action'
      ],
      research: 'City, E., et al., Instructional Rounds in Education (2009); EL Education, Leadership practices.'
    },
    {
      id: 'staff_culture',
      practice: 'Adult crew and staff culture',
      domain: 'leadership',
      description: 'Adults need crew too. EL schools build staff crews, regular check-ins, and rituals that mirror student crew. The premise: you cannot offer students what you do not experience yourself. Staff culture shapes student culture.',
      whyItMatters: 'Burnt-out adults cannot sustain a relational culture for students. Staff crew is not a perk; it is a precondition.',
      howlAlignment: ['compassion', 'responsibility'],
      classroomLook: 'A staff check-in at every meeting. Cross-role crews (teachers + custodians + counselors). Celebrations of staff growth. Norms for hard conversations.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Skipping staff crew when busy (rotation back into transactional)',
        'Performative wellness (yoga without time)',
        'Hierarchy preserved (admin not in staff crew)',
        'No safe space for dissent'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, The Power of Crew (2021); Brackett, M., Permission to Feel (2019).'
    },
    {
      id: 'two_way_feedback',
      practice: 'Two-way feedback culture',
      domain: 'culture',
      description: 'Feedback flows in all directions: teacher to student, student to teacher, teacher to leader, leader to teacher, peer to peer. Surveys, town halls, and check-ins normalize giving and receiving feedback as a routine professional skill.',
      whyItMatters: 'One-way feedback (top-down) builds compliance, not improvement. Two-way feedback builds trust and surfaces problems early.',
      howlAlignment: ['integrity', 'compassion'],
      classroomLook: 'Mid-trimester student surveys about teaching. Leader office hours for staff. Anonymous feedback channels. Public response to feedback received.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Surveys with no response (signals voice does not matter)',
        'Defensive reactions to critical feedback',
        'Anonymity used to harm rather than disclose',
        'Feedback collected only from the comfortable'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Feedback Cultures; Edmondson, A., The Fearless Organization (2018).'
    },
    {
      id: 'inclusive_design',
      practice: 'Inclusive design and UDL',
      domain: 'instruction',
      description: 'EL classrooms design with the margins in mind. Universal Design for Learning principles (multiple means of engagement, representation, and action) shape every lesson. Accommodations are built in, not bolted on. Disability is a normal part of human variation.',
      whyItMatters: 'Designing only for the median student excludes many. Designing for the margins benefits everyone, including students no one knew needed support.',
      howlAlignment: ['compassion', 'responsibility'],
      classroomLook: 'Multiple ways to access content (audio, video, text). Multiple ways to show what you know (write, draw, build, speak). Visual schedules. Sensory options. Honored identity in materials.',
      pitfalls: [
        'UDL as add-on for "those" students',
        'Accommodations announced publicly (embarrasses)',
        'Multiple options that all require the same skill',
        'No co-design with disabled students'
      ],
      research: 'CAST, Universal Design for Learning Guidelines (2018); EL Education, Inclusion practices.'
    },
    {
      id: 'culturally_responsive_curriculum',
      practice: 'Culturally responsive and sustaining curriculum',
      domain: 'curriculum',
      description: 'EL curriculum reflects the lives, histories, and languages of the students in front of it. Texts feature diverse authors. Expeditions investigate local and global topics that matter to students communities. Students home cultures are assets to build on, not obstacles to overcome.',
      whyItMatters: 'Students learn more from curriculum that reflects them. Students from dominant cultures also benefit from learning in a multivocal world.',
      howlAlignment: ['compassion', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'Classroom library with diverse authors. Expedition topics rooted in local community. Multilingual signage. Honoring of religious and cultural calendars.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Heroes-and-holidays tokenism',
        'Treating "diverse" as code for "non-white"',
        'Single-author canon plus a "diversity" unit',
        'No student input on curriculum'
      ],
      research: 'Ladson-Billings, G., The Dreamkeepers (1994); Paris, D. & Alim, S., Culturally Sustaining Pedagogies (2017); EL Education, Equity guidance.'
    },
    {
      id: 'multilingual_learners',
      practice: 'Multilingual learners as assets',
      domain: 'instruction',
      description: 'Students who speak languages other than English are treated as having a linguistic asset, not a deficit. Translanguaging is permitted in classrooms. Home languages appear in classroom materials. Bilingualism is celebrated as cognitive and cultural strength.',
      whyItMatters: 'Subtractive bilingualism (replacing home language with English) erases family connections and cognitive advantages. Additive bilingualism preserves both and produces stronger thinkers.',
      howlAlignment: ['compassion', 'integrity'],
      classroomLook: 'Word walls in multiple languages. Permission to draft in home language. Pairing newcomers with same-language buddies. Family translation policies.',
      pitfalls: [
        'English-only classroom rules',
        'Tracking ML students into low-rigor classes',
        'Underestimating cognitive ability based on English fluency',
        'No translated family communication'
      ],
      research: 'Garcia, O. & Wei, L., Translanguaging (2014); EL Education, Multilingual Learners (2019).'
    },
    {
      id: 'trauma_responsive',
      practice: 'Trauma-responsive practice',
      domain: 'culture',
      description: 'EL schools recognize that many students carry trauma that affects learning, behavior, and relationships. Trauma-responsive practice (predictability, choice, co-regulation, repair) is built into routines, not treated as a separate program. Behavior is communication.',
      whyItMatters: 'Trauma affects the brains capacity to learn. Schools that ignore trauma punish symptoms; schools that respond to trauma create the conditions for healing and learning.',
      howlAlignment: ['compassion', 'responsibility'],
      classroomLook: 'Predictable routines. Choice within structure. A calm-down corner. Co-regulating adults. Repair conversations after dysregulation, not punishment.',
      pitfalls: [
        'Diagnosing students (teachers are not clinicians)',
        'Lowered expectations framed as trauma response',
        'No self-care for adults (vicarious trauma)',
        'Trauma "trainings" without changes to practice'
      ],
      research: 'Van der Kolk, B., The Body Keeps the Score (2014); Souers, K. & Hall, P., Fostering Resilient Learners (2016); EL Education, Trauma-responsive crew.'
    }
  ];

declarations.name: CHARACTER_HABITS
declarations.source:
var CHARACTER_HABITS = [
    {
      id: 'compassion_habit',
      habit: 'Compassion',
      alsoCalled: ['kindness', 'caring', 'concern for others'],
      shortDef: 'Recognizing suffering and acting to relieve it.',
      whyItMatters: 'Compassion is the practical face of our shared humanity. Schools that cultivate compassion become safer, more connected, and more humane.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Notices when a classmate is sad and asks if they are okay.',
        level2: 'Consistently checks in with peers and offers specific support.',
        level3: 'Builds systems of care in the classroom and advocates for excluded peers without being asked.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Daily crew check-ins that practice noticing others',
        'Literature that builds perspective-taking',
        'Service learning with reflection on impact',
        'Restorative practices when harm happens',
        'Adults modeling compassion publicly',
        'Naming and celebrating compassionate acts'
      ],
      research: 'Goetz, J., et al., Compassion: An Evolutionary Analysis (2010); Keltner, D., Born to Be Good (2009).'
    },
    {
      id: 'empathy_habit',
      habit: 'Empathy',
      alsoCalled: ['perspective-taking', 'understanding others'],
      shortDef: 'Feeling with another person and accurately understanding their experience.',
      whyItMatters: 'Empathy precedes effective action. Without empathy, help becomes condescension and conflict becomes warfare.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Can name what a peer might be feeling in a familiar situation.',
        level2: 'Listens to understand before responding in conflict.',
        level3: 'Brings perspectives of the absent into discussions and decisions.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Perspective-taking protocols in discussion',
        'Diverse texts and primary sources',
        'Role-play of multiple perspectives',
        'Reflection on times we were misunderstood',
        'Empathy interviews in research projects',
        'Naming empathy as a skill, not a personality trait'
      ],
      research: 'Decety, J. & Ickes, W., The Social Neuroscience of Empathy (2009); Brown, B., Atlas of the Heart (2021).'
    },
    {
      id: 'courage_habit',
      habit: 'Courage',
      alsoCalled: ['bravery', 'guts', 'fortitude'],
      shortDef: 'Acting on values in the presence of fear.',
      whyItMatters: 'Without courage, integrity and compassion stay private. Courage is the bridge between values and action.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Tries something new even when nervous.',
        level2: 'Speaks up when a peer is being treated unfairly.',
        level3: 'Takes consistent action on principles even when costly socially or personally.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Public presentations that stretch comfort safely',
        'Stories of courage across cultures',
        'Discussion of difficult topics with structure',
        'Restorative repair after social rupture',
        'Adults sharing their own courage practice',
        'Distinguishing courage from recklessness'
      ],
      research: 'Pury, C. & Lopez, S., The Psychology of Courage (2010).'
    },
    {
      id: 'integrity_habit',
      habit: 'Integrity',
      alsoCalled: ['honesty', 'wholeness', 'authenticity'],
      shortDef: 'Aligning action with values consistently across contexts.',
      whyItMatters: 'Integrity is the foundation of trust. Without it, relationships and institutions cannot hold.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Tells the truth in small moments (admits a mistake on a worksheet).',
        level2: 'Acts the same when adults are not watching as when they are.',
        level3: 'Holds to principles under social pressure including from peer groups.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Honor codes co-created with students',
        'Restorative practices when integrity is broken',
        'Stories of integrity across cultures',
        'Adults modeling integrity including admitting mistakes',
        'Public commitments and follow-through',
        'Reflection on times integrity was hard'
      ],
      research: 'Damon, W., The Moral Child (1988); EL Education, Habits of Character.'
    },
    {
      id: 'respect_habit',
      habit: 'Respect',
      alsoCalled: ['regard', 'dignity', 'honor'],
      shortDef: 'Treating self and others as inherently worthy of dignity.',
      whyItMatters: 'Respect is the precondition for community. Without it, learning suffers and relationships fracture.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Uses respectful language with peers and adults.',
        level2: 'Treats those with less status (younger students, custodians) with the same respect as those with more.',
        level3: 'Maintains respect even in disagreement and conflict.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Classroom norms co-created with students',
        'Modeling respectful disagreement',
        'Restorative repair after disrespect',
        'Curriculum building awareness of dignity across difference',
        'Adults practicing respect across hierarchy',
        'Naming respect as practice, not feeling'
      ],
      research: 'Sennett, R., Respect in a World of Inequality (2003).'
    },
    {
      id: 'responsibility_habit',
      habit: 'Responsibility',
      alsoCalled: ['accountability', 'ownership', 'follow-through'],
      shortDef: 'Owning the impact of ones actions and following through on commitments.',
      whyItMatters: 'Responsibility is what makes us trustworthy and effective. It is also how we contribute to communities larger than ourselves.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Brings materials, completes assignments, manages basic tasks.',
        level2: 'Follows through on commitments to peers and adults consistently.',
        level3: 'Takes responsibility for shared outcomes and repairs when commitments are missed.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Goal-setting and progress monitoring',
        'Cooperative learning with assigned roles',
        'Crew responsibilities that rotate',
        'Restorative practices when commitments are broken',
        'Modeling responsibility including repair when adults miss commitments',
        'Service learning with real community accountability'
      ],
      research: 'EL Education, Habits of Character; Sergiovanni, T., Building Community in Schools (1994).'
    },
    {
      id: 'self_discipline',
      habit: 'Self-discipline',
      alsoCalled: ['self-control', 'self-regulation'],
      shortDef: 'Choosing long-term goals over short-term impulses.',
      whyItMatters: 'Self-discipline predicts a range of life outcomes more reliably than intelligence does. It is also teachable.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Resists distractions during focused work for short periods.',
        level2: 'Plans longer-term work and follows the plan.',
        level3: 'Manages competing demands and impulses across extended timeframes.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Goal-setting tied to personal values',
        'Time-management instruction explicit and practiced',
        'Reflection on what helps and hinders focus',
        'Choice in tasks to build intrinsic motivation',
        'Co-regulation strategies for dysregulation',
        'Adults modeling their own self-discipline practices'
      ],
      research: 'Duckworth, A. & Seligman, M., Self-Discipline Outdoes IQ (2005); Mischel, W., The Marshmallow Test (2014).'
    },
    {
      id: 'grit_habit',
      habit: 'Grit',
      alsoCalled: ['perseverance', 'tenacity', 'stick-to-it-iveness'],
      shortDef: 'Sustained passion and effort toward long-term goals.',
      whyItMatters: 'Long-term goals require sustained effort across years. Grit is what carries us through the boring middle of important work.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Returns to a hard task after a setback.',
        level2: 'Sustains effort across weeks or months on a chosen goal.',
        level3: 'Maintains a long-term passion through multiple setbacks and adjustments.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Long-term projects with real audiences',
        'Goal-setting with personal meaning',
        'Stories of grit across cultures',
        'Productive struggle as a value',
        'Crew support during long arcs',
        'Reflection on what sustains effort'
      ],
      research: 'Duckworth, A., Grit (2016). Caveat: Critics note grit research is correlational, may underweight structural barriers, and can be misused to blame students for systemic obstacles.'
    },
    {
      id: 'resilience_habit',
      habit: 'Resilience',
      alsoCalled: ['bounce-back', 'recovery'],
      shortDef: 'Recovering from setback and returning to engagement.',
      whyItMatters: 'Setbacks are inevitable. Resilience is what determines whether they become catastrophes or chapters.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Recovers from small setbacks (lost game, bad grade) within a class period.',
        level2: 'Recovers from larger setbacks (failed project, social rupture) within a week.',
        level3: 'Recovers from significant setbacks (loss, rejection) over appropriate time using self-knowledge.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Stories of resilience across cultures',
        'Crew as a recovery space',
        'Co-regulating adults',
        'Routines that hold steady through change',
        'Mental health literacy across grades',
        'Permission to feel without rushing recovery'
      ],
      research: 'Masten, A., Ordinary Magic (2014); Souers, K. & Hall, P., Fostering Resilient Learners (2016).'
    },
    {
      id: 'mindfulness_habit',
      habit: 'Mindfulness',
      alsoCalled: ['present-moment awareness', 'attention'],
      shortDef: 'Noticing present experience without immediate reaction or judgment.',
      whyItMatters: 'Mindfulness builds the gap between stimulus and response, the space in which choice lives.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Notices a strong feeling before acting on it sometimes.',
        level2: 'Pauses regularly to check in with self before reacting.',
        level3: 'Maintains awareness across the day and uses it to respond rather than react.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Brief breathing practices in crew',
        'Mindfulness as a tool, not a religion',
        'Naming feelings as practice',
        'Reflection routines',
        'Adults practicing and modeling mindfulness',
        'Choice of mindfulness forms across cultures'
      ],
      research: 'Kabat-Zinn, J., Wherever You Go, There You Are (1994); Schonert-Reichl, K., et al., Mindfulness in Schools (2015). Caveat: Mindfulness programs have mixed evidence and should not be deployed as the sole response to trauma or significant mental health needs.'
    },
    {
      id: 'adaptability_habit',
      habit: 'Adaptability',
      alsoCalled: ['flexibility', 'agility'],
      shortDef: 'Adjusting effectively to changing circumstances.',
      whyItMatters: 'Change is constant. Adaptability lets us thrive in uncertainty rather than be paralyzed by it.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Adjusts to small changes in routine without dysregulation.',
        level2: 'Reframes setbacks as new opportunities productively.',
        level3: 'Navigates significant life changes while maintaining values and effectiveness.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Routines that build security plus practice with change',
        'Reflection on adapting in the past',
        'Project work that requires adjustment',
        'Stories of adaptation across cultures',
        'Adults modeling adaptation including admitting struggle',
        'Permission to take time to adjust'
      ],
      research: 'Pulakos, E., et al., Adaptability in the Workplace (2000).'
    },
    {
      id: 'creativity_habit',
      habit: 'Creativity',
      alsoCalled: ['imagination', 'inventiveness', 'originality'],
      shortDef: 'Generating novel ideas, products, or solutions that have value.',
      whyItMatters: 'Many problems require new solutions. Creativity is also intrinsically valuable as human flourishing.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Generates multiple ideas when invited.',
        level2: 'Pursues a creative project sustained across days or weeks.',
        level3: 'Develops a distinctive creative voice across multiple works.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Open-ended tasks with multiple valid solutions',
        'Time for divergent thinking',
        'Models of creative work across cultures',
        'Safety to try and fail',
        'Adults sharing their own creative work',
        'Studio time across disciplines'
      ],
      research: 'Csikszentmihalyi, M., Creativity (1996); Robinson, K., Out of Our Minds (2001).'
    },
    {
      id: 'innovation_habit',
      habit: 'Innovation',
      alsoCalled: ['problem-solving', 'invention'],
      shortDef: 'Applying creativity to solve real problems in useful ways.',
      whyItMatters: 'Creativity becomes innovation when it meets a real problem. Both are needed in a complex world.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Identifies a small problem and proposes a solution.',
        level2: 'Develops and tests a solution to a real problem across weeks.',
        level3: 'Iterates a solution based on feedback and brings it to actual use.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Design thinking processes',
        'Real-problem projects with stakeholders',
        'Prototyping and iteration cycles',
        'Stories of innovation including failures',
        'Adults sharing their own problem-solving',
        'Time and tools for making'
      ],
      research: 'Brown, T., Change by Design (2009); EL Education, Project-Based Learning.'
    },
    {
      id: 'critical_thinking_habit',
      habit: 'Critical thinking',
      alsoCalled: ['analytical thinking', 'reasoning'],
      shortDef: 'Examining evidence, weighing perspectives, and forming reasoned judgments.',
      whyItMatters: 'In an information-saturated world, the ability to evaluate and reason carefully is more valuable than ever.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Distinguishes fact from opinion.',
        level2: 'Evaluates sources for credibility.',
        level3: 'Constructs and defends arguments with evidence and revises position when warranted.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Source-based research',
        'Argument writing',
        'Socratic seminars',
        'Media literacy across disciplines',
        'Modeling teacher inquiry and uncertainty',
        'Discussion of multiple credible perspectives'
      ],
      research: 'Paul, R. & Elder, L., Critical Thinking (2006); Common Core argument standards.'
    },
    {
      id: 'quality_habit',
      habit: 'Quality',
      alsoCalled: ['excellence', 'craft'],
      shortDef: 'Producing work that meets a meaningful standard of beauty, accuracy, and care.',
      whyItMatters: 'Quality is not snobbery; it is care made visible. Students who experience quality develop standards that serve them across life.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Cares enough to revise a single piece.',
        level2: 'Cares about quality across multiple pieces without being told.',
        level3: 'Pursues quality as a personal standard regardless of grade.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Models of excellence dissected with students',
        'Critique and revision routines',
        'Real audiences',
        'Time for revision',
        'Adults producing and sharing their own quality work',
        'Co-created rubrics'
      ],
      research: 'Berger, R., An Ethic of Excellence (2003); EL Education, Models of Excellence.'
    },
    {
      id: 'craftsmanship_habit',
      habit: 'Craftsmanship',
      alsoCalled: ['skill', 'mastery'],
      shortDef: 'Developing depth of skill in a chosen practice over time.',
      whyItMatters: 'Craftsmanship is what makes mastery possible. It also produces a kind of pride and identity that no shortcut delivers.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Develops a basic skill (writing, drawing, building) with intention.',
        level2: 'Sustains craft development over months in a chosen form.',
        level3: 'Develops distinctive personal craft over years.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Time for sustained practice',
        'Mentors and masters in chosen fields',
        'Studio culture in classrooms',
        'Models of craft across cultures',
        'Public display and use of crafted work',
        'Tools and materials of real quality'
      ],
      research: 'Sennett, R., The Craftsman (2008); Berger, R., An Ethic of Excellence (2003).'
    },
    {
      id: 'service_habit',
      habit: 'Service',
      alsoCalled: ['contribution', 'giving back'],
      shortDef: 'Acting on behalf of others and the common good.',
      whyItMatters: 'Service builds the muscles of citizenship and connects students to communities larger than themselves.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Participates in classroom or school service tasks.',
        level2: 'Sustains service to a community organization across weeks or months.',
        level3: 'Initiates service in response to a community need they identified.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Service learning tied to academic work',
        'Partnerships with community organizations',
        'Reflection on impact and reciprocity',
        'Stories of service across cultures',
        'Adults modeling service',
        'Recognition of service without prizes'
      ],
      research: 'Eyler, J. & Giles, D., Wheres the Learning in Service-Learning? (1999).'
    },
    {
      id: 'citizenship_habit',
      habit: 'Citizenship',
      alsoCalled: ['civic engagement', 'public participation'],
      shortDef: 'Active participation in the civic and political life of communities.',
      whyItMatters: 'Democracy requires participants, not spectators. Citizenship is how individuals shape the conditions of common life.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Knows basic civic structures and participates in class and school decisions.',
        level2: 'Engages with local civic issues and structures.',
        level3: 'Sustains civic engagement including advocacy and (when eligible) voting.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Civics across grades',
        'Student government with real authority',
        'Voter education and pre-registration',
        'Local civic engagement projects',
        'Discussion of current issues with multiple perspectives',
        'Visits from elected officials and civic leaders'
      ],
      research: 'Levinson, M., No Citizen Left Behind (2012); CIRCLE youth civic research.'
    },
    {
      id: 'equity_habit',
      habit: 'Equity',
      alsoCalled: ['fairness', 'justice'],
      shortDef: 'Distributing opportunity and resources so all can thrive.',
      whyItMatters: 'Equity is different from equal treatment: it accounts for different starting points and removes barriers. It is foundational to a just society.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Notices when resources or opportunities are distributed unfairly.',
        level2: 'Acts to share opportunities fairly within their own circles.',
        level3: 'Advocates for equity beyond their own interests including challenging unfair systems.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Curriculum that includes equity analysis',
        'Practice noticing power and privilege',
        'Discussion of equity in classroom and school decisions',
        'Adults modeling equity practice',
        'Service learning rooted in equity',
        'Honest engagement with histories of inequity'
      ],
      research: 'Hammond, Z., Culturally Responsive Teaching and the Brain (2015); EL Education, Equity guidance.'
    },
    {
      id: 'anti_racism_habit',
      habit: 'Anti-racism',
      alsoCalled: ['racial equity', 'racial justice'],
      shortDef: 'Active recognition and resistance of racism in self, others, and systems.',
      whyItMatters: 'Racism shapes American institutions including schools. Anti-racism is the active practice that distinguishes participation from complicity.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Recognizes racist language and behavior and does not participate.',
        level2: 'Speaks up when witnessing racism in peer settings.',
        level3: 'Engages in sustained anti-racist work including examining own racial identity and acting on systemic issues.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Honest curriculum about racial history and present',
        'Diverse texts and perspectives',
        'Practice with restorative conversations after racial harm',
        'Adults doing their own anti-racism work publicly',
        'Affinity spaces where appropriate',
        'Action on school-level racial equity issues'
      ],
      research: 'Kendi, I., How to Be an Antiracist (2019); Hammond, Z., Culturally Responsive Teaching and the Brain (2015). Caveat: Anti-racism work is contested in some communities; be transparent with families about curriculum and engage with critique in good faith.'
    },
    {
      id: 'environmental_stewardship',
      habit: 'Environmental stewardship',
      alsoCalled: ['sustainability', 'ecological responsibility'],
      shortDef: 'Caring for the natural world as a member of its systems.',
      whyItMatters: 'Climate change and ecosystem disruption are defining challenges for this generation. Stewardship is how we live as part of natural systems rather than against them.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Practices basic conservation behaviors (turning off lights, reducing waste).',
        level2: 'Engages with environmental issues in school and community.',
        level3: 'Sustains environmental action across years including advocacy and personal practice.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Fieldwork in natural settings',
        'Place-based curriculum',
        'School sustainability practices',
        'Environmental science across grades',
        'Connection with local environmental groups',
        'Honest engagement with climate science and emotion'
      ],
      research: 'Sobel, D., Place-Based Education (2004); EL Education, Environmental practices.'
    },
    {
      id: 'global_awareness_habit',
      habit: 'Global awareness',
      alsoCalled: ['global citizenship', 'international perspective'],
      shortDef: 'Understanding oneself as part of a global community with global responsibilities.',
      whyItMatters: 'Local and global are increasingly connected. Global awareness lets students navigate this reality with both humility and effectiveness.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Recognizes that people elsewhere live differently and meaningfully.',
        level2: 'Understands global systems (trade, climate, migration) that shape lives.',
        level3: 'Engages with global issues with sustained inquiry and action.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Curriculum including global perspectives',
        'Texts in translation',
        'Virtual or in-person exchanges',
        'Global current events integrated into routines',
        'Cross-cultural fieldwork when possible',
        'Adults sharing their global engagement'
      ],
      research: 'Reimers, F., Empowering Global Citizens (2017).'
    },
    {
      id: 'cultural_humility',
      habit: 'Cultural humility',
      alsoCalled: ['cross-cultural respect', 'cultural openness'],
      shortDef: 'Engaging across cultures with awareness of ones own limits and respect for others expertise on their own experience.',
      whyItMatters: 'Cultural competence claims expertise; cultural humility claims learning. The latter is more honest and more productive.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Asks rather than assumes about unfamiliar cultural practices.',
        level2: 'Recognizes own cultural assumptions as one perspective among many.',
        level3: 'Sustains cross-cultural relationships with mutual learning and challenges own bias actively.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Curriculum that includes diverse cultural perspectives',
        'Practice asking rather than assuming',
        'Reflection on own cultural identity',
        'Adults modeling cultural humility',
        'Engagement with cultural critique without defensiveness',
        'Authentic cross-cultural relationships when possible'
      ],
      research: 'Tervalon, M. & Murray-Garcia, J., Cultural Humility (1998).'
    },
    {
      id: 'spiritual_literacy_secular',
      habit: 'Spiritual literacy (secular)',
      alsoCalled: ['existential literacy', 'meaning-making'],
      shortDef: 'Engaging with questions of meaning, purpose, and the transcendent without imposing or excluding particular religious traditions.',
      whyItMatters: 'Humans across cultures have asked questions about meaning. Schools that ignore these questions leave students unprepared for them; schools that impose answers violate religious freedom. Literacy is the middle path.',
      threeLevelExamples: {
        level1: 'Recognizes that humans across cultures ask big questions about meaning.',
        level2: 'Engages thoughtfully with diverse traditions of meaning-making.',
        level3: 'Develops own meaning-making practice while respecting others.'
      },
      cultivation: [
        'Literature and primary sources from diverse religious and secular traditions',
        'Discussion of big questions without single right answers',
        'Visits to places of worship and contemplation across traditions',
        'Reflection practices drawn from multiple traditions with student choice',
        'Adults sharing their own meaning-making with appropriate boundaries',
