declarations.name: EL_RESEARCH
declarations.source:
var EL_RESEARCH = [
    {
      id: 'mathematica_2013',
      title: 'EL Education impact on achievement: Mathematica study',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2013,
      summary: 'A three-year quasi-experimental study by Mathematica Policy Research examined EL Education schools in five districts. Students in EL schools showed significantly higher reading achievement than matched comparison students, with effects equivalent to roughly 7-10 months of additional learning.',
      whatItShows: 'Sustained implementation of EL practices is associated with measurable academic gains, particularly in literacy.',
      practiceImplication: 'EL practices implemented with fidelity over multiple years can deliver substantial academic gains.',
      caveat: 'Quasi-experimental design has selection bias risks despite matching. Implementation fidelity varies across schools. Schools voluntarily adopted EL, suggesting unobserved differences.',
      citation: 'Nichols-Barrer, I. & Haimson, J., Mathematica Policy Research (2013). Annual study report at edresearchforaction.org and mathematica.org archives.'
    },
    {
      id: 'crew_attendance_research',
      title: 'Advisory and student outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2014,
      summary: 'Multiple studies of advisory programs (similar to EL Crew structure) show positive associations with attendance, behavior referrals, and student-reported sense of belonging when implemented consistently with sustained adult-student relationships.',
      whatItShows: 'Structural advisory time with a consistent adult correlates with better student outcomes, especially in middle school transition years.',
      practiceImplication: 'Crew is not extra; it is structural. The same adult over multiple years matters more than the curriculum content of crew time.',
      caveat: 'Effects depend heavily on implementation quality. Advisory programs done poorly show no effect or negative effect on student perception.',
      citation: 'Galassi, J., et al., Strengths-Based School Counseling (2008); reviews of middle school advisory programs.'
    },
    {
      id: 'project_based_learning_meta',
      title: 'Project-based learning and student outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2021,
      summary: 'A meta-analysis of high-quality project-based learning studies found small to moderate positive effects on academic achievement and stronger effects on engagement and content retention compared to traditional instruction. Effects are stronger for sustained, well-designed projects.',
      whatItShows: 'Project-based learning, including expedition learning, can produce academic gains alongside engagement gains when implementation is high-quality.',
      practiceImplication: 'Expeditions need design rigor, teacher support, and time. Short or poorly designed projects do not produce the same effects.',
      caveat: 'Meta-analyses show wide variation in PBL definitions and quality. Short-term gains may not match long-term retention claims across studies.',
      citation: 'Chen, C. & Yang, Y., Revisiting the effects of project-based learning, Educational Research Review (2019).'
    },
    {
      id: 'deeper_learning_outcomes',
      title: 'Deeper learning network outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2014,
      summary: 'American Institutes for Research studied schools in the Deeper Learning Network (including EL Education schools) and found students reported higher engagement, completed more rigorous coursework, and had higher college enrollment rates than matched peers.',
      whatItShows: 'Schools emphasizing deeper learning, including project-based and authentic work, can support stronger post-secondary trajectories.',
      practiceImplication: 'Engagement and authentic work do not require sacrificing academic rigor; the two reinforce each other.',
      caveat: 'Network schools self-selected and had additional support. Effects may not generalize to schools attempting deeper learning without infrastructure.',
      citation: 'Zeiser, K., et al., American Institutes for Research, Evidence of Deeper Learning Outcomes (2014).'
    },
    {
      id: 'character_education_meta',
      title: 'Character education and outcomes meta-analysis',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2011,
      summary: 'A meta-analysis of social-emotional learning programs (213 studies, 270,000+ students) found significant positive effects on social-emotional skills, attitudes, behavior, and academic performance. Effects on academic achievement averaged 11 percentile points.',
      whatItShows: 'Well-designed character and SEL programs produce measurable benefits including academic gains, not at the expense of academics.',
      practiceImplication: 'Investing in character development (HOWLs) is not a tradeoff against academic achievement; it supports it.',
      caveat: 'Meta-analysis includes many program types of varying quality. EL Education was not specifically isolated. Effects depend heavily on implementation.',
      citation: 'Durlak, J., et al., The Impact of Enhancing Students Social and Emotional Learning, Child Development (2011).'
    },
    {
      id: 'student_led_conferences_research',
      title: 'Student-led conferences and engagement',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2010,
      summary: 'Studies of student-led conferences show increases in family attendance at conferences (compared to traditional parent-teacher), student-reported ownership of learning, and student self-efficacy. Implementation quality matters substantially.',
      whatItShows: 'Putting students in the lead of conferences shifts who owns the learning conversation and can engage families who otherwise do not attend.',
      practiceImplication: 'Student-led conferences require preparation, portfolio work, and adult restraint. Done well, they produce measurable shifts.',
      caveat: 'Most research is qualitative or quasi-experimental. Effects on academic outcomes are inferred rather than directly demonstrated.',
      citation: 'Bailey, J. & Guskey, T., Implementing Student-Led Conferences (2001); EL Education internal evaluations.'
    },
    {
      id: 'expeditionary_learning_high_school',
      title: 'EL Education high school outcomes',
      source: 'EL Education',
      yearPublished: 2018,
      summary: 'EL Education has documented graduation rates, college enrollment rates, and persistence rates at network high schools that match or exceed comparable schools. Some EL high schools serving high-needs populations show especially notable outcomes.',
      whatItShows: 'EL Education schools, including those serving historically underserved students, can produce strong post-secondary outcomes.',
      practiceImplication: 'EL practices scale to high school and can support college and career readiness for diverse student populations.',
      caveat: 'Internal evaluation by program developer requires external validation. Network schools have varied implementation quality.',
      citation: 'EL Education Annual Report (2018); network high school outcome data.'
    },
    {
      id: 'critique_revision_research',
      title: 'Critique and revision effects on writing',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2008,
      summary: 'Research on revision and peer feedback in writing instruction shows that students who engage in multiple drafts with structured peer critique produce higher-quality final work than students who write single drafts, even with teacher feedback.',
      whatItShows: 'The critique-revise cycle improves writing quality more than single drafts with teacher feedback alone.',
      practiceImplication: 'Time for revision is essential. Peer critique with structure can supplement, not replace, teacher feedback.',
      caveat: 'Effects depend on critique quality. Untrained peer critique can be unhelpful or harmful. Time tradeoffs are real.',
      citation: 'Topping, K., Peer Assessment, Theory Into Practice (2009).'
    },
    {
      id: 'restorative_practices_meta',
      title: 'Restorative practices effects',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2018,
      summary: 'Reviews of restorative practices in schools show reductions in suspensions, particularly for Black and Latino students, and improvements in school climate. Effects on academic achievement are mixed and depend on implementation quality.',
      whatItShows: 'Restorative practices can reduce discipline disparities and improve school climate when well-implemented.',
      practiceImplication: 'Restorative practices require training, time, and culture shift. Done as add-on or replacement for skill-building, they show weaker results.',
      caveat: 'Restorative practices implemented poorly (without staff training, without skill-building) can backfire. Some studies show null or mixed effects on academics.',
      citation: 'Gregory, A. & Evans, K., The Promise of Restorative Practices to Transform Teacher-Student Relationships, AERA Open (2020).'
    },
    {
      id: 'fieldwork_outcomes',
      title: 'Outdoor and field-based learning outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2017,
      summary: 'Studies of field-based and outdoor learning show positive effects on student engagement, retention of content, environmental knowledge, and pro-environmental behavior. Effects are stronger for repeated field experiences than single trips.',
      whatItShows: 'Fieldwork is not just enrichment; it produces measurable learning gains and behavioral effects.',
      practiceImplication: 'Sustained fieldwork tied to curriculum is more valuable than occasional field trips.',
      caveat: 'Research is largely descriptive and short-term. Long-term retention and transfer are less well-studied.',
      citation: 'Becker, C., et al., Effects of regular classes in outdoor education, International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (2017).'
    },
    {
      id: 'culturally_responsive_meta',
      title: 'Culturally responsive teaching and outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2017,
      summary: 'A meta-review of culturally responsive teaching research found positive effects on student engagement, sense of belonging, and academic outcomes, particularly for students of color. Effects depend on depth of implementation.',
      whatItShows: 'Culturally responsive practice produces measurable benefits especially for students whose cultures are typically marginalized in schools.',
      practiceImplication: 'Surface-level cultural responsiveness (heroes and holidays) does not produce the effects of substantive practice.',
      caveat: 'Research base mixes many definitions of "culturally responsive." Some effects are inferred from related constructs (e.g., teacher-student relationships).',
      citation: 'Aronson, B. & Laughter, J., The theory and practice of culturally relevant education, Review of Educational Research (2016).'
    },
    {
      id: 'family_engagement_meta',
      title: 'Family engagement and student outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2002,
      summary: 'The classic A New Wave of Evidence synthesis of 51 family engagement studies found consistent positive effects on student achievement, attendance, behavior, and post-secondary trajectory. Effects are strongest when engagement is two-way and sustained.',
      whatItShows: 'Family-school partnerships are a leverage point with strong evidence of impact on student outcomes.',
      practiceImplication: 'Investing in family partnerships pays dividends across multiple student outcomes. One-way communication is much weaker.',
      caveat: 'Effects depend on family engagement type. Some forms (homework help) show weaker effects than others (high expectations, school involvement).',
      citation: 'Henderson, A. & Mapp, K., SEDL, A New Wave of Evidence (2002).'
    },
    {
      id: 'productive_struggle_research',
      title: 'Productive struggle in mathematics',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2007,
      summary: 'Research on mathematics instruction shows that students who engage in productive struggle (working through difficulty without immediate rescue) demonstrate stronger conceptual understanding and retention than students who receive immediate teacher solutions.',
      whatItShows: 'Productive struggle is a key driver of conceptual learning, particularly in mathematics.',
      practiceImplication: 'Teacher restraint matters. Wait time, student-to-student discussion before teacher answer, and tolerance for confusion support learning.',
      caveat: 'Unproductive struggle (too hard, no entry point) does not produce these effects. The art is calibrating challenge.',
      citation: 'Hiebert, J. & Grouws, D., The effects of classroom mathematics teaching on students learning (2007).'
    },
    {
      id: 'self_assessment_research',
      title: 'Self-assessment and academic achievement',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2009,
      summary: 'Visible Learning meta-analysis identifies student self-assessment and self-reported grades as among the highest-effect-size interventions in education (d > 1.0). Students who accurately self-assess and set goals show stronger achievement.',
      whatItShows: 'When students learn to assess their own work accurately, they learn more.',
      practiceImplication: 'Routine self-assessment is not extra; it is a high-leverage instructional practice.',
      caveat: 'Effect size is highest when self-assessment is accurate and tied to action. Inaccurate or perfunctory self-assessment shows weaker effects.',
      citation: 'Hattie, J., Visible Learning (2009).'
    },
    {
      id: 'goal_setting_research',
      title: 'Goal-setting and student outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2002,
      summary: 'Decades of research on goal-setting (Locke and Latham) show that specific, challenging goals produce higher performance than vague goals or no goals. Effects are mediated by effort, persistence, and strategy development.',
      whatItShows: 'Goal-setting is an evidence-based practice across domains including education.',
      practiceImplication: 'Specific, challenging, student-owned goals tied to action produce stronger effects than generic goals.',
      caveat: 'Goal-setting can produce narrowing of focus and ethical lapses if not designed thoughtfully (overemphasis on measurable goals).',
      citation: 'Locke, E. & Latham, G., Building a Practically Useful Theory of Goal Setting, American Psychologist (2002).'
    },
    {
      id: 'classroom_relationships_meta',
      title: 'Teacher-student relationships and outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2011,
      summary: 'A meta-analysis of teacher-student relationship quality found significant positive effects on engagement and achievement, with effect sizes comparable to direct instruction effects. Effects are especially strong for at-risk students.',
      whatItShows: 'Relationship is not separate from learning; it is a substantial driver of it.',
      practiceImplication: 'Investments in relationship-building (crew, advisory, sustained adult-student relationships) are academic investments.',
      caveat: 'Causal direction is hard to establish. Some effects may be from selection (better-relating teachers also have better instruction).',
      citation: 'Roorda, D., et al., The influence of affective teacher-student relationships on students school engagement and achievement, Review of Educational Research (2011).'
    },
    {
      id: 'authentic_audience_research',
      title: 'Authentic audience and writing quality',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2010,
      summary: 'Studies of writing instruction show that students who write for real audiences beyond the teacher produce higher-quality writing with more revision than students who write for the teacher alone. Effects are mediated by motivation and care.',
      whatItShows: 'Audience matters. Real audiences raise quality through raising stakes.',
      practiceImplication: 'EL Educations emphasis on public presentations and authentic audiences is supported by writing research.',
      caveat: 'Effects depend on the audience actually mattering. Token "authentic" audiences (a parent night with no real engagement) do not produce the same effects.',
      citation: 'Magnifico, A., Writing for whom? Cognition, motivation, and a writers audience, Educational Psychologist (2010).'
    },
    {
      id: 'middle_school_transition',
      title: 'Middle school transition and student outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2008,
      summary: 'Research on the middle school transition shows declines in motivation, engagement, and achievement for many students. Schools that maintain personalization through advisory and small learning communities mitigate these declines.',
      whatItShows: 'The middle school transition is a vulnerability point. Structures like crew protect against the typical decline.',
      practiceImplication: 'Crew is especially valuable in middle school grades when adolescents typically disengage.',
      caveat: 'Effects depend on the quality of personalization. Small schools or advisory structures without depth do not produce these effects.',
      citation: 'Eccles, J. & Roeser, R., Schools as developmental contexts during adolescence, Journal of Research on Adolescence (2011).'
    },
    {
      id: 'el_charter_outcomes',
      title: 'EL Education charter network outcomes',
      source: 'EL Education',
      yearPublished: 2019,
      summary: 'EL Education has published outcome data from network charter schools showing graduation, college enrollment, and persistence rates above state averages and serving largely low-income and historically marginalized student populations.',
      whatItShows: 'EL Education model produces strong outcomes in schools serving diverse and high-needs populations.',
      practiceImplication: 'EL practices are not just for affluent schools; they have shown effects in high-needs settings.',
      caveat: 'Internal data; charter selection effects possible. Network schools have additional supports not available to all adopters.',
      citation: 'EL Education Annual Outcomes Reports (2019, 2020, 2021).'
    },
    {
      id: 'engagement_achievement_link',
      title: 'Engagement-achievement relationship',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2004,
      summary: 'Decades of research on student engagement establish strong correlations between behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement and academic achievement. Engagement is increasingly recognized as both outcome and mediator of achievement.',
      whatItShows: 'Engagement and achievement are tightly linked. Investing in engagement supports achievement.',
      practiceImplication: 'Engagement is not separate from academics; engaging instruction is academic instruction.',
      caveat: 'Causal direction can run both ways. High-achievers may be more engaged because of mastery, not necessarily the reverse.',
      citation: 'Fredricks, J., Blumenfeld, P., Paris, A., School engagement: Potential of the concept, state of the evidence, Review of Educational Research (2004).'
    },
    {
      id: 'service_learning_outcomes',
      title: 'Service learning and student outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2011,
      summary: 'A meta-analysis of service learning programs found significant positive effects on academic outcomes, civic engagement, and social-emotional skills. Effects are stronger for programs with strong academic linkage and reflection.',
      whatItShows: 'Service learning done well produces academic, civic, and SEL benefits simultaneously.',
      practiceImplication: 'Service hours alone are weaker than academically-linked service with reflection. EL Educations service learning approach matches research.',
      caveat: 'Implementation quality varies widely. Token service projects show weaker effects.',
      citation: 'Celio, C., Durlak, J., Dymnicki, A., A meta-analysis of the impact of service-learning on students, Journal of Experiential Education (2011).'
    },
    {
      id: 'arts_integration_research',
      title: 'Arts integration and academic outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2013,
      summary: 'Research on arts integration in academic subjects shows positive effects on student engagement, content retention, and in some studies academic achievement. Effects are stronger for sustained integration than occasional arts experiences.',
      whatItShows: 'Arts are not extra; integrated arts can support core academic learning.',
      practiceImplication: 'EL Educations emphasis on craft and quality of work across disciplines including arts is supported by integration research.',
      caveat: 'Some claims of arts effects on transfer (music improves math) are overstated. Specific arts integration into specific subjects has clearer effects than general claims.',
      citation: 'Robinson, A., Arts integration and the success of disadvantaged students, Arts Education Policy Review (2013).'
    },
    {
      id: 'trauma_informed_outcomes',
      title: 'Trauma-informed schools and outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2018,
      summary: 'Emerging research on trauma-informed school approaches shows improvements in attendance, behavior referrals, and school climate. Academic effects are mixed and depend heavily on implementation depth.',
      whatItShows: 'Trauma-informed practice has consistent effects on relational and behavioral outcomes; academic effects require deeper implementation.',
      practiceImplication: 'Surface-level "trauma trainings" do not produce the effects of integrated practice changes (routines, co-regulation, restorative response).',
      caveat: 'Trauma-informed implementation is uneven; some studies show null effects. Distinguishing trauma-informed culture from compensatory programming matters.',
      citation: 'Maynard, B., et al., Trauma-Informed Approaches in Schools: A Systematic Review, Campbell Collaboration (2019).'
    },
    {
      id: 'cooperative_learning_meta',
      title: 'Cooperative learning meta-analyses',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2009,
      summary: 'Decades of cooperative learning research (Johnson and Johnson) show consistent positive effects of structured cooperative learning over individualistic or competitive learning on academic, social, and psychological outcomes.',
      whatItShows: 'Cooperative learning with structure outperforms unstructured group work and individual work for most learning goals.',
      practiceImplication: 'Cooperative learning protocols matter; unstructured "group work" does not produce the same effects.',
      caveat: 'Effects depend on protocols used. Some teachers call any group work "cooperative learning" without the structure that produces effects.',
      citation: 'Johnson, D., Johnson, R., Stanne, M., Cooperative learning methods: A meta-analysis (2000); ongoing reviews.'
    },
    {
      id: 'feedback_research',
      title: 'Feedback effects on learning',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2007,
      summary: 'Hattie and Timperley meta-analyses identify feedback as a top-tier instructional practice when feedback is specific, actionable, and tied to clear targets. Praise feedback has weaker effects than task-specific feedback.',
      whatItShows: 'Feedback can be powerful but is not automatically so; what makes it powerful is specificity, focus on the task, and actionability.',
      practiceImplication: 'Kind, specific, helpful is research-grounded. Vague praise ("good job") shows weaker effects.',
      caveat: 'Some forms of feedback (grades alone) have weak or negative effects. Feedback delivered poorly can hurt rather than help.',
      citation: 'Hattie, J. & Timperley, H., The power of feedback, Review of Educational Research (2007).'
    },
    {
      id: 'reading_engagement_research',
      title: 'Reading engagement and achievement',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2008,
      summary: 'Reading engagement research shows that engaged readers read more, develop stronger vocabulary, and have higher reading achievement. Engagement is supported by interesting texts, choice, social interaction around texts, and authentic purposes.',
      whatItShows: 'Reading engagement is both outcome and driver of reading achievement.',
      practiceImplication: 'EL Educations emphasis on engaging, complex texts with discussion supports the engagement-achievement loop.',
      caveat: 'Engagement is hard to measure precisely. Some research relies on student self-report.',
      citation: 'Guthrie, J., et al., Reading engagement and achievement, Engaged Reading (1999); subsequent reviews.'
    },
    {
      id: 'civic_engagement_youth',
      title: 'Civic education and youth outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2013,
      summary: 'CIRCLE and other youth civic research shows that students with high-quality civic education are more likely to vote, volunteer, and engage in civic action as adults. Action-based civic education has stronger effects than civics knowledge alone.',
      whatItShows: 'Civic education matters for future civic engagement, and action-based civic learning matters more than knowledge alone.',
      practiceImplication: 'EL Educations service learning and authentic civic engagement align with research on what builds civic habits.',
      caveat: 'Long-term causal claims are hard to establish. Self-selection into civic education programs can confound effects.',
      citation: 'CIRCLE research at Tufts; Levinson, M., No Citizen Left Behind (2012).'
    },
    {
      id: 'place_based_research',
      title: 'Place-based education outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2014,
      summary: 'Place-based education research shows positive effects on student engagement, sense of place, environmental knowledge, and in some studies on academic achievement. Effects are stronger when place-based work is sustained.',
      whatItShows: 'Place-based learning produces engagement and environmental literacy benefits and can support academic learning.',
      practiceImplication: 'EL Educations emphasis on local expeditions and fieldwork is supported by place-based learning research.',
      caveat: 'Research base is smaller than for other practices. Causal claims often rely on small qualitative studies.',
      citation: 'Sobel, D., Place-Based Education (2004); Place-Based Education Evaluation Collaborative reports.'
    },
    {
      id: 'multilingual_learners_research',
      title: 'Multilingual learners and additive bilingualism',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2017,
      summary: 'Decades of research on multilingual learners shows that maintaining and developing home language alongside English (additive bilingualism) produces better long-term academic and cognitive outcomes than English-only approaches.',
      whatItShows: 'Home language is an asset for learning English and for cognitive development overall.',
      practiceImplication: 'Translanguaging, home-language acknowledgment, and bilingual education where possible are evidence-based.',
      caveat: 'Implementation varies. Some "bilingual" programs are weak in execution. Research is clearest on long-term outcomes; short-term test scores may show different patterns.',
      citation: 'Collier, V. & Thomas, W., Educating English Learners for a Transformed World (2009); Garcia, O., Bilingual Education in the 21st Century (2009).'
    },
    {
      id: 'school_climate_meta',
      title: 'School climate and student outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2013,
      summary: 'Meta-analyses of school climate research find consistent positive associations between positive climate and student outcomes including academic achievement, behavior, mental health, and attendance.',
      whatItShows: 'School climate is a foundational variable that affects many outcomes simultaneously.',
      practiceImplication: 'Investments in school climate (crew, relationships, restorative practices, beautiful environments) pay dividends across outcomes.',
      caveat: 'Climate is multidimensional and hard to measure. Reverse causality (better outcomes produce better climate) is possible.',
      citation: 'Thapa, A., et al., A review of school climate research, Review of Educational Research (2013).'
    },
    {
      id: 'professional_learning_research',
      title: 'Professional learning communities and student outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2008,
      summary: 'Research on professional learning communities shows positive effects on teaching practice and, in some studies, student outcomes when PLCs include shared norms, focus on student learning, collective inquiry, and time for sustained collaboration.',
      whatItShows: 'Teacher collaboration with structure can improve practice and student outcomes.',
      practiceImplication: 'EL Educations emphasis on teacher teams, looking at student work together, and shared expedition design is supported by PLC research.',
      caveat: 'PLCs done as compliance with no shared purpose show weaker effects. Time alone is not enough.',
      citation: 'Vescio, V., Ross, D., Adams, A., A review of research on the impact of professional learning communities, Teaching and Teacher Education (2008).'
    },
    {
      id: 'identity_safe_classrooms',
      title: 'Identity-safe classrooms and outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2014,
      summary: 'Research on identity-safe classrooms shows that environments where students identities (race, culture, language, gender, ability) are honored as assets produce stronger academic and social outcomes than identity-neutral or identity-threat environments.',
      whatItShows: 'Identity safety is foundational to learning, particularly for students whose identities are typically marginalized in schools.',
      practiceImplication: 'EL Educations equity work is academic work; identity-safe practice supports academic outcomes.',
      caveat: 'Identity-safe is harder to operationalize than to describe. Surface-level "diversity" practices do not produce identity safety.',
      citation: 'Steele, D. & Cohn-Vargas, B., Identity Safe Classrooms (2013).'
    },
    {
      id: 'longitudinal_character_research',
      title: 'Character development and long-term outcomes',
      source: 'external research',
      yearPublished: 2015,
      summary: 'Longitudinal research on character development including conscientiousness, self-discipline, and prosocial behavior shows associations with adult outcomes including educational attainment, employment, health, and relationship quality.',
      whatItShows: 'Character traits cultivated in childhood and adolescence are associated with adult flourishing across multiple domains.',
      practiceImplication: 'Investing in character is investing in long-term life outcomes, not just short-term school behavior.',
      caveat: 'Longitudinal correlation does not establish causation; underlying genetic and environmental factors may drive both. Definitions of character vary across studies.',
      citation: 'Heckman, J., et al., Hard evidence on soft skills, Labour Economics (2012); Roberts, B., et al., personality and life outcomes research.'
    }
  ];
